title: CSC3710 2026-09-01: Recursive Definitions (Natural Numbers, Addition, Sets of Strings)

questions.q: Which three parts make up a recursive definition of a set?
questions.explain: Basis: finitely many starting elements. Recursive step: operations that build new elements from ones already in the set. Closure: nothing else belongs to the set.

questions.q: How many elements does the basis of a recursive definition put into the set?
choices: None; the basis only lists operations
questions.explain: The basis declares a finite number of elements to be in S. For example, the even-length definition has only λ, and the odd-length definition has a and b.

questions.q: What does the closure part of a recursive definition of a set S say?
choices: An element is in S only if it is a basis element or can be obtained from basis elements by a finite number of applications of the recursive-step operations
Every string over the alphabet is in S
The recursive step may be applied only once
S is closed under every operation, including ones not listed in the recursive step
questions.explain: Closure means nothing else is in S. Only the elements you can actually build, in finitely many steps, belong to the set.

questions.q: Without the closure part, the basis and recursive step only say that at least certain elements are in the set, so a larger set (such as the set of all strings) would also satisfy them.
questions.explain: The basis and recursive step guarantee which elements are in the set. Closure is what keeps everything else out, so the set contains exactly the buildable elements.

questions.q: Writing "0, 1, 2, 3, ..." is a precise definition of the natural numbers, because the pattern is obvious.
questions.explain: The "..." is imprecise because the reader has to guess the pattern. Recursive definitions exist so that sets with infinitely many elements can be defined precisely.

questions.q: When developing a mathematical theory such as the theory of languages, the theorems and proofs may use only what?
choices: The definitions of the concepts of that theory, so both the objects and the operations need precise definitions
Any fact that is intuitively obvious
Results computed with ordinary arithmetic on numerals
Examples that have been checked by hand
questions.explain: Inside a theory you may use only its definitions, so you need precise definitions of the objects of the domain (e.g. the natural numbers) and the operations (e.g. addition).

questions.q: According to the textbook view shown in this lecture, which disciplines do the theoretical foundations of computer science come from?
choices: Electrical engineering (tools used in electricity and electromagnetism)
questions.explain: The four are logic, electrical engineering, brain research and linguistics. It was also noted that quantum computing now brings in quantum mechanics, beyond electromagnetism.

questions.q: Which of the foundational disciplines is the source of formal languages and grammars, the area associated with Noam Chomsky?
questions.explain: Linguistics (Chomsky) gives us formal languages and grammars.

questions.q: The natural numbers N are defined with basis 0 ∈ N. What is the recursive step?
choices: If n ∈ N, then s(n) ∈ N
If n ∈ N, then n + 1 ∈ N
If s(n) ∈ N, then n ∈ N
If n ∈ N, then n + n ∈ N
questions.explain: N is built with the successor operation s, so its elements are 0, s(0), s(s(0)), and so on. At this point neither + nor numerals like 1 exist.

questions.q: Which pair of equations is the recursive definition of addition (basis; recursive step)?
choices: m + 0 = m;  m + s(n) = s(m + n)
m + 0 = m;  m + s(n) = s(m) + s(n)
m + 0 = s(m);  m + s(n) = m + n
questions.explain: Basis: adding 0 to a natural gives the same natural. Recursive step: peel one s off the right operand and move it outside the sum.

questions.q: Apply the recursive step of addition once to s(s(s(0))) + s(s(0)). What do you get?
questions.explain: Here m = s(s(s(0))) and the right operand is s(n) with n = s(0). The step m + s(n) = s(m + n) moves one s outside the whole sum. It doesn't move it into the left operand, and it doesn't swap the operands.

questions.q: Use the recursive definition of addition to compute s(s(0)) + s(0). Write the final answer with s and 0 only (e.g. s(s(0))).
questions.explain: s(s(0)) + s(0) = s( s(s(0)) + 0 ) by the recursive step, then = s( s(s(0)) ) = s(s(s(0))) by the basis. Check: 2 + 1 = 3.

questions.q: How many applications of the recursive step are needed to compute s(0) + s(s(s(s(0)))) with the definition of addition?
questions.explain: You need one recursive step for each s in the right operand. There are four, and then the basis is applied once.

questions.q: When computing s(s(s(0))) + s(s(s(s(s(0))))) step by step, how many times is the basis (m + 0 = m) applied?
questions.explain: Five recursive steps bring the right operand down to 0. Then one basis step removes the + 0, giving eight s's (3 + 5 = 8).

questions.q: To save steps when computing s(s(s(0))) + s(s(s(s(s(0))))), you may first rewrite it as s(s(s(s(s(0))))) + s(s(s(0))).
questions.explain: Commutativity (m + n = n + m) is a theorem that hasn't been proven at this "beginning of the world". Only the definitions may be used, so the operands stay as given.

questions.q: Which expression can the basis of addition be applied to directly?
questions.explain: The basis covers only m + 0, with 0 on the right. 0 + s(s(0)) needs two recursive steps first, because "0 + n = n" isn't part of the definition.

questions.q: When is a derivation using the definition of addition finished?
choices: When the expression contains no +, only s's and 0
After exactly one recursive step and one basis step
When the result can be written as a numeral like 6
questions.explain: Repeat the recursive step until the right operand is 0, then apply the basis. The answer is a natural with no addition left in it. Numerals are only for checking your work.

questions.q:
A student computes s(s(0)) + s(s(0)) as follows. Which line does NOT follow from the definition of addition?
(1) = s( s(s(0)) + s(0) )
(2) = s( s(s(s(0))) + 0 )
(3) = s( s(s(s(0))) )
questions.explain: Line (2) moves the s into the left operand. The recursive step, applied inside the parentheses, gives s( s( s(s(0)) + 0 ) ), with the s outside the sum. The final value happens to be right, but the step isn't justified by the definition.

questions.q: The definition of multiplication is built using the definition of addition.
questions.explain: That's how the theory grows: new concepts are defined from ones that are already defined.

questions.q: Someone answers "What is 3 + 1?" with "2 + 2". What point does this illustrate about formal definitions?
choices: Formally there is no built-in notion of a "simplified" form; the same issue comes up with regular expressions
The answer is wrong because 2 + 2 is a different natural number
Addition is undefined when both operands are nonzero
Every expression has exactly one correct way to be written
questions.explain: 2 + 2 is correct but unexpected. Nothing in the formal setting says which expression counts as "simplified". For addition you know you're finished because the result has no +.

questions.q: Basis: a ∈ K, b ∈ K. Recursive step: if t ∈ K then ttt ∈ K. Closure. Which set is K?
choices: Strings of only a's or only b's whose length is a power of 3 (1, 3, 9, 27, ...)
All strings over {a, b} whose length is a multiple of 3
All strings of only a's or only b's
questions.explain: a, b → aaa, bbb → a^9, b^9 → a^27, b^27, ... Each step triples the length, and all three copies of t are the same string.

questions.q: Basis: a ∈ K, b ∈ K. Recursive step: if t ∈ K then ttt ∈ K. Closure. Which strings are in K?
questions.explain: K holds a^1, a^3, a^9, a^27, ... and the same powers of b. aba and ab would need different values of t in one rule, and a^6 has length 6, which isn't a power of 3.

questions.q: In the rule "if t ∈ K then ttt ∈ K", the three t's may be replaced by three different elements of K.
questions.explain: A variable has one value per rule application, so every t is the same string. To combine different elements you need a second variable, e.g. "if t ∈ K and w ∈ K then tw ∈ K".

questions.q: Basis: λ ∈ K. Recursive step: if t ∈ K then atb ∈ K. Closure. What are the four shortest elements of K?
questions.explain: λ → aλb = ab → a·ab·b = aabb → aaabbb. K is a^n b^n for n ≥ 0.

questions.q: Basis: λ ∈ K. Recursive step: if t ∈ K then ta, at, btb ∈ K. Which strings does the first execution of the recursive step (t = λ) produce?
questions.explain: λa = a, aλ = a (a repetition, which is fine), and bλb = bb. This definition gives the strings with an even number of b's.

questions.q: Basis: a ∈ K. Recursive step: if t ∈ K then tt ∈ K. Closure. Which string is in K?
questions.explain: a → aa → aaaa → a^8 → ... Each step doubles the length, so the lengths are powers of 2.

questions.q: Even-length strings are defined by basis λ ∈ K and rules taa, tab, tba, tbb. How many distinct strings of length 4 does the second execution of the recursive step produce?
questions.explain: The first execution gives the 4 strings of length 2. Appending each of the 4 two-symbol blocks to each of those gives 2·2·2·2 = 16 strings of length 4, which is all of them.

questions.q: How many strings of length 5 are there over the alphabet {a, b}?
questions.explain: There are 2^n strings of length n over a two-symbol alphabet, and 2^5 = 32.

questions.q: The recursive definitions of even-length and odd-length strings over {a, b} use the same rules (taa, tab, tba, tbb). What is different?
choices: Only the basis: λ for even length, and a and b for odd length
The odd-length definition needs an extra rule ta
The odd-length definition uses ttt instead of the four append rules
questions.explain: Appending a two-symbol block keeps the parity of the length, so the basis decides the set. Starting from a and b, the first execution gives all 8 strings of length 3.

questions.q: In the second execution of the recursive step, what do you apply the rules to?
choices: Every element that was new in the first execution, using every rule (a table with t-values as rows and rules as columns helps)
Only the longest element generated so far
questions.explain: The basis elements were already used in the first execution, so the second execution applies every rule to each element that was new in the first.

questions.q: The empty string λ belongs to the set of even-length strings over {a, b}.
questions.explain: λ has length 0, and 0 is even. It's the shortest element, so it goes in the basis.

questions.q: Proposed definition of even-length strings: basis λ ∈ K; if t ∈ K then t·t·a ∈ K and t·t·b ∈ K. Which generated string shows the definition is wrong?
questions.explain: With t = λ, the rule gives λ·λ·a = a, which has odd length 1. One generated string outside the target set is enough to disprove the definition.

questions.q: A recursive definition of K is meant to define a target set S. Which of these show that the definition is wrong?
choices: It generates a string that is not in S
Some string in S can never be generated
Some string is generated twice by different routes
One of its rules only produces strings the other rules already produce
questions.explain: A definition can be wrong in two ways: it makes too much (unsound) or too little (incomplete). Repetitions and redundant rules aren't errors.

questions.q: One counterexample is enough to show that a recursive definition does not define the intended set.
questions.explain: A single generated string outside the set, or a single string in the set that can never be generated, disproves the definition. No proof is needed.

questions.q: If a program generates all strings of a definition up to length 6 and they match the target set exactly, the definition has been proven correct.
questions.explain: Matching short strings is evidence, not proof. Proving S = K needs structural induction.

questions.q: What kind of proof is needed to formally show that a recursively defined set K equals a described set S?
choices: Proof by listing the first few elements
Direct computation with the definition of addition
questions.explain: Structural induction is a version of mathematical induction for recursively defined sets. A counterexample can only disprove S = K.

questions.q: Why must the shortest element of the target set go in the basis when the only operation is concatenation?
choices: Concatenation only makes strings longer, so nothing shorter can be generated later
Closure requires the basis to contain exactly one element
The recursive step can't be applied to the shortest element
The basis must contain every element of the set
questions.explain: Every rule builds a longer string from an existing one. If the shortest element isn't in the basis, no rule can ever produce it.

questions.q: Which is a correct recursive definition of the odd-length strings over {a, b}?
choices: Basis a, b ∈ K; if t ∈ K then taa, tab, tba, tbb ∈ K
Basis λ ∈ K; if t ∈ K then taa, tab, tba, tbb ∈ K
Basis a ∈ K; if t ∈ K then taa, tab, tba, tbb ∈ K
Basis a, b ∈ K; if t ∈ K then ta, tb ∈ K
questions.explain: Basis λ gives the even-length strings. Basis a alone only gives odd-length strings that start with a, so b is missing. The rules ta, tb generate all nonempty strings, including even-length ones like ab.

questions.q: The string ab belongs to the set of strings over {a, b} with an odd number of a's.
questions.explain: ab has one a, which is odd. It has even length, so don't confuse "odd number of a's" with "odd length".

questions.q: How many strings of length 4 over {a, b} have an odd number of a's?
questions.explain: For n ≥ 1 there are 2^(n-1) of them: choose the first n-1 symbols freely, and the last symbol is forced. The eight are abbb, babb, bbab, bbba, aaab, aaba, abaa, baaa.

questions.q: Target set: strings with an odd number of a's. Basis a ∈ K. Which rule is unsound (it generates a string outside the set)?
questions.explain: With t = a, the rule ta gives aa, which has two a's. The other rules add 0 or 2 a's, so the count stays odd.

questions.q: Basis a ∈ K. Recursive step: if t ∈ K then tb, taa, bt ∈ K. Which strings does the first execution of the recursive step produce?
questions.explain: With t = a: tb = ab, taa = aaa, bt = ba. bab only shows up in the second execution, from t = ab with bt or from t = ba with tb.

questions.q: Basis a ∈ K with rules tb, taa, bt only. Which string has an odd number of a's but can never be generated?
questions.explain: aaba starts with a (so not from bt), ends with a (so not from tb), and doesn't end in aa (so not from taa). The others work: abaa = ab·aa, baaa = b·aaa, aaab = aaa·b. ababa, used in class, fails for the same reason.

questions.q: Adding the rule ata to the rules tb, taa, bt (basis a) lets ababa be generated. Which derivation produces ababa?
questions.explain: ata wraps t in two a's, which keeps the count odd. a·bab·a = ababa. The other derivations don't apply the rules correctly.

questions.q: With basis a ∈ K, the three rules tb, bt and ata alone correctly define the set of strings with an odd number of a's.
questions.explain: Each rule adds 0 or 2 a's, so they're sound. They're also complete: a string that ends in b comes from tb, one that starts with b comes from bt, and one that starts and ends with a comes from ata. The rules taa and aat are redundant but harmless.

questions.q: With basis a and rules tb, taa, bt, the string bab is produced twice in the second execution (from t = ab with bt, and from t = ba with tb). This repetition makes the definition wrong.
questions.explain: Generating the same string by different routes isn't an error. What makes rules tb, taa, bt wrong is that they're incomplete: they miss strings like aaba.
